planting.note: Divide and press small mats into consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; meadow spikemoss is a low, moss-like native groundcover that spreads naturally in damp lawns, ditches, and woodland-edge meadows across the eastern and southeastern US.

directions: Divide and press small mats into consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring, firming them into contact with the ground so the trailing stems can root along their length. Meadow spikemoss forms a soft, bright-green, moss-like carpet of tiny scale-leaved stems that creep along damp ground in wet meadows, ditch banks, and the shaded edges of lawns throughout the eastern and southeastern United States, staying low enough to tolerate light foot traffic and occasional mowing. It spreads readily once established in reliably moist soil, making it a useful low-maintenance groundcover for a damp shaded spot where turfgrass struggles, though it thins out quickly if the soil is allowed to dry for extended periods. Keep it consistently watered through the first season and top-dress lightly with compost; established patches need little further care beyond occasional edging to keep them within bounds.

planting.note: Divide and transplant in early spring before fronds fully unfurl, into well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; upland brittle fern grows naturally on rocky wooded slopes and talus rather than the damp bottomland preferred by the closely related lowland bladder fern.

directions: Divide and transplant in early spring before fronds fully unfurl, siting the fern in well-drained, humus-rich soil tucked among rocks or on a sloped woodland bank in partial to full shade. Upland brittle fern forms a delicate, finely cut, light-green clump that closely resembles the lowland bladder fern but favors drier, rockier upland woods and talus slopes rather than damp valley bottoms, and its fronds are especially brittle and easily snapped at the stem base, a trait shared across the genus. It is summer-deciduous in drought, dying back when conditions turn hot and dry and re-emerging with cooler, moister fall weather, so do not mistake dormancy for plant loss. A good choice for a shaded rock garden or the dry edge of a woodland border where richer, constantly moist soil is not available.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated crowns in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade in fall, when this species' evergreen sterile frond emerges; like other grapeferns it depends on soil mycorrhizae and is slow to establish from division.

directions: Plant nursery-propagated crowns in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade in fall, since this fern's single, finely divided, lacy sterile frond emerges in autumn and stays green through winter before withering the following summer, an unusual schedule opposite most ferns. A separate beaded fertile spike, when present, rises alongside the sterile blade in late summer or fall and releases spores that depend on a long, hidden underground partnership with soil fungi before a new plant appears, so division and transplant success is slow and unpredictable. It grows scattered through open deciduous woods, old fields, and woodland edges across much of the eastern and southeastern United States, more often noticed for its handsome winter foliage than for size, since mature plants rarely exceed ten inches. Treat it as a patient, long-term addition to a shaded woodland floor rather than a fast-establishing groundcover, and avoid disturbing the soil around planted crowns.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated crowns in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade in fall, when the evergreen sterile frond emerges; southern grapefern is the Gulf Coast's common winter-green grapefern, found in shaded pine-hardwood duff from the Carolinas to Texas.

directions: Plant nursery-propagated crowns in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade in fall, since the finely cut, lacy, evergreen sterile frond of southern grapefern emerges in autumn and persists through the winter months, going dormant again by early summer. It is the common warm-climate counterpart to the more northern cutleaf grapefern, found scattered through the leaf litter of shaded pine-hardwood woods and old fields across the Gulf and South Atlantic coastal plain, where its beaded, grape-cluster-like fertile spike appears alongside the sterile blade in fall. Like other grapeferns it depends on an unseen, long-lived partnership with soil mycorrhizal fungi, so transplants establish slowly and unpredictably and are best treated as a patient, low-disturbance addition to a shaded native woodland floor rather than a plant grown for quick effect.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated crowns in consistently moist, sandy, humus-rich soil in partial shade to filtered sun in fall; bulbous adder's-tongue is the smallest and earliest-emerging of the Gulf Coast adder's-tongue ferns, common in damp lawns, moist pastures, and open sandy woods from the Carolinas to Texas.

directions: Plant nursery-propagated crowns in consistently moist, sandy, humus-rich soil in partial shade to filtered sun in fall; bulbous adder's-tongue is the tiniest member of its genus in the region, its single small, rounded, undivided blade barely an inch or two tall arising each winter from a small underground bulb-like stem, with a short fertile spike beside it bearing a row of spore cases. It appears briefly in the cool, wet season in damp lawns, moist sandy pastures, and open pine woods across the Gulf and South Atlantic coastal plain, then withers away by late spring, making it easy to overlook among grass and low groundcover. Like other adder's-tongues it relies on a long-term underground mycorrhizal relationship, so newly planted crowns take time to settle in and should not be disturbed once sited. Best suited to a damp, lightly shaded corner of a native lawn alternative or woodland-edge planting where its brief winter appearance can be enjoyed up close.
